questions.q: When scoring a pillar against the ZTMM stages, why does the lesson recommend starting from the Optimal definition and working backward?
options: CISA requires assessments to be documented in descending order
It forces you to prove each stage is genuinely true in production until you reach one where the honest answer is yes
It is the only order the scoring spreadsheet template supports
Starting from Traditional would take longer because it has more sub-criteria
questions.explain: Working backward from Optimal forces an honest stop at the highest stage you can actually prove with evidence, rather than defaulting upward to where you'd like to be.

questions.q: In the worked Identity example, why isn't the pillar simply scored as 'Advanced' once phishing-resistant MFA and automated risk scoring are live?
options: Because CISA does not recognize Advanced as a valid score for the Identity pillar
Because Advanced requires removing passwords entirely, which the example never discusses
Because phishing-resistant MFA only counts toward the Devices pillar, not Identity
Because service accounts and some legacy apps still bypass those controls, so the gap needs to be recorded explicitly rather than rounded up
questions.explain: The example is mostly Advanced but has a documented coverage gap in legacy apps and non-human identity — the lesson's point is to record that gap explicitly, not smooth it into a single rounded-up label.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a maturity score should reflect the 'floor' rather than an average across strong and weak areas?
options: An organization's real exposure tracks its weakest material gap, since that's the door an attacker can actually walk through
Averages are mathematically impossible to compute across four ordinal stages
The floor is always easier to measure than an average
CISA's published model explicitly forbids averaging as a scoring method
questions.explain: In the Devices example, one showcase application or managed fleet with strong controls doesn't offset an unmanaged BYOD population with no compliance signal — the real risk tracks the weaker, uncontrolled path.

questions.q: Why is 'we're migrating to this next year' not valid evidence for this quarter's maturity score?
options: Migration plans are automatically scored as Traditional regardless of content
Migration plans can only be used to score the Networks pillar
A planned future state is not evidence of current behavior in production — it belongs in the roadmap conversation, not today's score
CISA only accepts evidence submitted in the following fiscal year
questions.explain: Scoring to the plan instead of the evidence is one of the common mistakes the lesson flags — intent for next year doesn't change what's actually true in production today.

questions.q: What is the main reason the lesson warns against 'scoring the tool, not the behavior'?
options: Tools are scored under a separate maturity model maintained by vendors, not CISA
Owning a capable platform (like PAM) doesn't mean the rollout is complete — maturity depends on whether the behavior is actually enforced across the real population
Behavior-based scoring is required only for the Data pillar
Tool-based scoring always produces a lower score than behavior-based scoring
questions.explain: Owning a PAM platform doesn't make you Advanced on Identity if half your admin accounts still have standing access because the rollout never finished — maturity is measured by enforced behavior, not purchased capability.
